headline: Canarsie Pier and Cross Bay Bridge: the two doors into Jamaica Bay right now
subhead: Snapper blues and weakfish are keeping rods bent while the bunker build that should trigger the fall run keeps thickening in the back bay.
body_markdown:
If you've only got a few hours this week, pick your access point by what you want to catch, because the bay is splitting into two different games right now. Canarsie Pier is the play for anyone fishing with light tackle or bringing a kid along — the rail there is loaded with snapper blues and blowfish, and it's also the best free seat in the house for watching bunker density build along the mud flats. Cross Bay Bridge and the Beach Channel side, whether you're working it from a kayak or a small boat, is where the fluke and weakfish game is still alive on the channel edges. Two different access points, two different reasons to use them, and both worth knowing depending on what your Saturday looks like.

The bigger story for the week is bait. Bunker schools have been building steadily in the back bay — off Ruler's Bar, in Grassy Bay, and pushing toward the Rockaway Inlet side — and that's exactly the pattern we flagged last week: those schools concentrating are what sets up the first real fall striper push. It hasn't tipped yet. Stripers in the bay are still in a holding pattern, scattered rather than schooled, which lines up with what's happening region-wide — bass are present but not committed anywhere until the bait balls up tighter. With the moon building toward full over the next several days, tidal flow increases, and that's usually the mechanism that finally squeezes bait into blitz-worthy pods. Watch the mouth of the inlet and the flats off Breezy Point closely over the next week to ten days. That's where this transitions from "scattered bass around bait" to something worth planning a trip around.

Fluke fishing has done what it typically does at the end of August — it's softened, not collapsed. Warm water sitting in the shallower flats has pushed the better fish toward the inlet and toward the deeper channel structure where there's more current and cooler, better-oxygenated water. That's a seasonal transition, not a sign the season's over — expect fluke to stay catchable on structure and in the deeper channels right through September before they slide out toward the ocean side for good. Right now the better drifts are along the edges of Beach Channel and the deeper cuts near Cross Bay Bridge, working white or chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, worked slow along the bottom on the last two hours of the outgoing. A few boats working the flats off Ruler's Bar Hassock have also picked at fluke mixed in with weakfish on the same presentation, just fished a little higher off bottom.

Weakfish have been the pleasant surprise piece of the bay puzzle this month, and they're still showing on those same channel edges — Grassy Bay, the flats off Big Egg Marsh, and the deeper water tight to the Cross Bay Bridge pilings. Small soft plastics on light jigheads, three to four inch pearl or bubblegum-colored paddletails, worked slow on the drift with the outgoing tide, have been drawing strikes. These aren't the big spring weakfish — mostly schoolies in the 14 to 18-inch range — but they're active and they're a nice change of pace when the fluke bite is soft.

Bluefish remain the most dependable predator in the bay right now, and that tracks with what's happening up and down the coast — warm water has kept them aggressive and spread out, and that's not likely to change through Labor Day week. Snapper blues are thick around Canarsie Pier and the Cross Bay Bridge shadow line, easy pickings on tiny Kastmasters or a sliver of spearing under a bobber, which makes for good action if you've got kids or you're breaking in someone new to the sport. Bigger bluefish, cocktail-sized and up, are working the Rockaway Inlet on the last of the ebb, chopping bunker on the surface some mornings. Poppers and bunker chunks fished on wire leader near the inlet mouth have been producing, especially in that first hour of light before the boat traffic picks up.

Porgies are still around if you want to put some fillets in the cooler — the structure at Beach Channel and around the Cross Bay Bridge pilings holds them on bloodworms or clam bait, fished on a simple high-low rig near bottom. Nothing spectacular, but a steady producer for anyone who wants a mixed bag day rather than chasing one species.

For the next few days, expect more of the same pattern — soft but catchable fluke on the channel edges, dependable snapper and cocktail blues inside the bay, weakfish holding on the flats, and bass still scattered rather than schooled. The moon and the building bunker are the two things to watch. If that bait tightens up the way it's trending, the first real blitz signs should start showing at the inlet and off Breezy Point within the next week to ten days — that's when Marine Parkway Bridge starts to matter again, working the swirling water under the span on the outgoing with bucktails or swimmers after dark. Until then, work the access points that are actually producing, and keep an eye on the bunker.
